name: Acetyl hexapeptide-3
lead: Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the older name for the cosmetic peptide now listed under the INCI name acetyl hexapeptide-8 and sold as Argireline. It is a six-amino-acid fragment (Ac-Glu-Glu-Met-Gln-Arg-Arg-NH2) of SNAP-25, a protein involved in neurotransmitter release [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that the "-3" name is considered incorrect for this peptide, although it persists in older papers, patents and product listings [1].

People use it in serums and creams aimed at expression lines, especially the forehead and the crow's-feet area around the eyes. The idea is that by dampening the small repeated muscle contractions behind frown and squint lines, the skin looks smoother over weeks of daily use, giving a gentler, needle-free counterpart to botulinum toxin injections [1][6]. It is usually layered into an ordinary skincare routine alongside moisturisers, retinoids or hyaluronic acid.

The original 2002 paper reported wrinkle-depth reductions of up to 30% after 30 days on volunteers using an emulsion with 10% of the peptide [6]. Later randomized studies in Chinese and other volunteers have reported improvements in periorbital wrinkle appearance [10], while Wikipedia and a 2025 review it cites describe inconsistent statistical results across studies and no head-to-head comparison with botulinum toxin [1]. Its size and water-loving chemistry limit skin penetration, which has prompted work on microneedle patches and iontophoresis [3][4].

paras: Acetyl hexapeptide-3 corresponds to residues 12 to 17 of the N-terminal region of SNAP-25. The acetylated N-terminus and amidated C-terminus are described as protecting the short chain from enzymatic breakdown [2]. It is produced entirely by chemical (solid-phase) peptide synthesis and has no natural source [2]. Its molecular weight of roughly 889 Da is far above the size usually associated with easy skin absorption [1][3].

Wikipedia lists several names for the same molecule: acetyl hexapeptide-8 amide, Argireline, Argireline acetate, EEMQRR and the older acetyl hexapeptide-3 [1]. Cosmetic labels use the INCI name acetyl hexapeptide-8, while many academic papers, including microneedle delivery work, still use acetyl hexapeptide-3 or AHP-3 [3][4][5].

The peptide is marketed for dynamic wrinkles: lines created by repeated muscle movement such as frowning or squinting. Product copy and reviews describe it as a topical option for people who want a smoother forehead and eye area without injections [1][8]. Grokipedia reports typical cosmetic use at concentrations up to around 0.005% in finished products, and notes that formulators combine it with agents such as hyaluronic acid or retinol [2].

Review authors place peptides such as Argireline among the commonly used cosmeceuticals for photoaging alongside botanicals and hydroquinone [21]. Aesthetic clinicians also describe pairing cosmeceuticals with chemical peels, lasers and injectables to support results and shorten recovery [11].

Registered studies have tested acetyl hexapeptide-8 for blepharospasm, an involuntary eyelid-muscle disorder, and for the look of oily skin [7][8][12]. A 2023 report proposed embedding it in absorbable polydioxanone (PDO) threads used in facial lifting, with the aim of releasing the peptide into the upper face over time [13].

The peptide mimics the N-terminal region of SNAP-25 and is proposed to compete for a place in the SNARE complex, reducing vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction [1][2]. The 2002 paper reported that in cell experiments it reduced neurotransmitter release with a potency comparable to botulinum toxin A but with much lower maximal efficacy, as expected of a small peptide [6]. Botulinum toxin acts on the same machinery, by cleaving SNAP-25 [1]. No clinical study has compared the two directly, and the effective concentration is unclear [1].

Researchers describe poor skin permeation due to molecular weight and hydrophilicity; a 2015 study cited by Wikipedia found under 0.2% of an applied dose reached the outer skin layer after 24 hours [1]. Experimental microneedle patches, 3D-printed personalised microneedle eye patches, microneedle pretreatment and iontophoresis have been studied to improve delivery [3][4][14]. Analytical work has also measured how much peptide actually appears in commercial creams and serums, since labelled content can differ between products [15].

Wikipedia reports availability since 2001 and a 2002 paper in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science introducing it as an anti-wrinkle peptide, which described it as the product of a rational design programme aimed at a non-toxic mimic of botulinum toxin's action [1][6]. Grokipedia (AI-generated) attributes its development to the Barcelona company Lipotec, later part of Lubrizol, and describes it as an early cosmetic peptide aimed at neurotransmitter release [2].

Patent filings from the mid-2000s combine acetyl hexapeptide-3 with vitamin A derivatives in creams, nano-emulsions and solid anti-wrinkle sticks [16][17][18]. A 2024 longitudinal analysis of search and social interest tracked public attention to the ingredient as it spread through skincare media [19].

The 2002 original study reported up to 30% reduction in wrinkle depth after 30 days in women using a 10% peptide emulsion, with no oral toxicity or primary skin irritation at high doses in the safety tests described [6].

A randomized, placebo-controlled study in 60 Chinese subjects applied the cream or placebo to periorbital wrinkles twice daily for 4 weeks in a 3:1 ratio. The abstract reports a total subjective efficacy of 48.9% in the Argireline group versus 0% with placebo, with objective silicone-replica analysis also reported [10].

A 2017 randomized study of 24 volunteers tested acetyl hexapeptide-3 alone and with tripeptide-10 citrulline over 60 days; the authors reported antiwrinkle activity and reduced transepidermal water loss for acetyl hexapeptide-3 [5]. A registered phase 3 study of periorbital wrinkles enrolled 70 people, and a small study of oily-skin appearance enrolled 14 [7][12]. Studies of acetyl hexapeptide-8 in blepharospasm were also registered, one of them terminated [8][20].

Wikipedia describes a 2012 pilot in blepharospasm in which the cream used alongside botulinum toxin injections prolonged symptom relief versus placebo, and a 2025 review noting that some studies show improved wrinkle appearance while statistical significance is inconsistent and multi-ingredient formulas give steadier results [1]. A 2024 systematic review of photoaging cosmeceuticals reported that the evidence base for peptides contained mostly Level Ib studies in its own grading [21]. Laboratory work on skin fibroblasts has tested it as part of peptide mixtures [9].

Wikipedia reports a 2012 study with no significant adverse effects and a later review stating that no serious adverse events have been reported, with lower potency and toxicity than botulinum toxin [1]. The Chinese randomized study and the original 2002 work also reported good tolerability [6][10]. A review of periocular aesthetic treatments documents ocular complications mainly for injectables and procedures rather than topical peptides [22].

Argireline became one of the best-known cosmetic peptides, marketed in the media as "needle-free Botox" [15]. Analytical chemists have taken up the framing as a measurement problem, developing methods to detect and quantify the peptide in finished creams and sera [15]. In the United States it is sold over the counter as a cosmetic ingredient [1].

card.summary: The older name for Argireline, the topical 'Botox-alternative' peptide with modest, inconsistent evidence.
card.note: Poor skin penetration; no direct comparison with botulinum toxin.

quick.overview:
Acetyl hexapeptide-3 is the older name of Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8), a cosmetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for expression lines.

Studies suggest it may improve the look of wrinkles, but results are inconsistent and hard to compare.
quick.mechanism: It copies a fragment of SNAP-25 and is proposed to interfere with the SNARE complex that triggers muscle-activating neurotransmitter release. Its poor skin absorption is an active research topic.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects in the cited studies were minimal. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold over the counter.

chain: Applied as a cream or serum around the eyes and forehead
Proposed to dampen the nerve signal that makes small facial muscles contract
Softer-looking expression lines over weeks of daily use
angle.text: Users apply it daily to the forehead and eye area to soften the look of frown and crow's-feet lines. Studies of the peptide in volunteers have reported reduced wrinkle depth or improved wrinkle grading over about 4 to 8 weeks [6][10].
